```{r setup}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(readr); library(dplyr); library(knitr); library(tibble) })
FIG <- function(file, width = "90%") {
  p <- file.path("..", "output", "figures", file)
  if (file.exists(p))
    cat(sprintf("\n\n::: {style=\"text-align:center;\"}\n![](%s){width=%s}\n:::\n\n", p, width))
  else
    cat("::: {.placeholder}\n<span class='ph-tag'>\u25a2 pending data</span><br>Figure pending: run the corresponding script (see README) to generate it.\n:::\n")
}
.rdc <- function(p) tryCatch(readr::read_csv(file.path("..","output",p), col_types = readr::cols(.default = "c")), error = function(e) NULL)
.sc <- .rdc("projections/bcr_scenarios_table.csv")
BCR_C <- if (!is.null(.sc)) .sc$BCR[grepl("^Central", .sc$Scenario)] else "1.0"
BCR_SK <- if (!is.null(.sc)) .sc$BCR[grepl("skills earnings premium", .sc$Scenario)] else "2.5"
.as <- .rdc("projections/bcr_assumptions.csv")
EMP_C <- if (!is.null(.as)) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*as.numeric(.as$Central[.as$Parameter == "Female labour force participation"])) else "52%"
.mc <- .rdc("models/mincer_ifls_controls.csv")
MINCER_C <- if (!is.null(.mc)) { v <- .mc$`Return per year`[.mc$Sex == "Women" & grepl("^\\(4\\)", .mc$Model)]; sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * as.numeric(v[1])) } else "9.6%"
.tn <- .rdc("projections/bcr_tornado.csv")
if (!is.null(.tn)) { .o <- .tn[!grepl("NEET|premium", .tn$Parameter), ]; .v <- as.numeric(c(.o$`BCR at low value`, .o$`BCR at high value`))
  RANGE_LO <- sprintf("%.2f", min(.v)); RANGE_HI <- sprintf("%.2f", max(.v)) } else { RANGE_LO <- "0.71"; RANGE_HI <- "1.57" }
.ef <- .rdc("models/followup_EF_changes.csv")
.chg <- function(u, col) { if (is.null(.ef)) return("n/a"); x <- as.numeric(.ef[[col]][.ef$unit == u])
  sprintf("%s %.1f points", ifelse(x < 0, "fell", "rose"), abs(x)) }
.en <- .rdc("models/followup2_B_secondary_enrolment.csv")
.enc <- function(u, s) { if (is.null(.en)) return(NA); r <- .en[.en$unit == u & .en$sex == s, ]
  as.numeric(r$rate[r$year == "2025"]) - as.numeric(r$rate[r$year == "2024"]) }
.ll <- .rdc("projections/lifetime_loss.csv")
.llv <- function(m) if (is.null(.ll)) NA else readr::parse_number(.ll$Value[grepl(m, .ll$Metric, fixed = TRUE)][1])
LOSS_BN <- sprintf("%.1f", .llv("TOTAL forgone lifetime productivity, East Java (USD)") / 1e9)
LOSS_GIRLS <- format(round(.llv("Excess NEET girls (gap x population)"), -3), big.mark = ",")
LOSS_PER <- format(round(.llv("PV of forgone lifetime earnings, per excess-NEET girl (USD)"), -2), big.mark = ",")
.sk <- if (!is.null(.sc)) .sc[grepl("skills earnings premium", .sc$Scenario), ][1, ] else NULL
.pn <- function(x) readr::parse_number(x)
RET_B <- if (!is.null(.sk)) .sk$`Retention benefit (USD/girl)` else "242"
SK_B  <- if (!is.null(.sk)) .sk$`Skills premium benefit (USD/girl)` else "365"
TOT_B <- if (!is.null(.sk)) .sk$`Total benefit (USD/girl)` else "607"
COST  <- if (!is.null(.sk)) .sk$`Cost (USD/girl)` else "200"
SK_ONLY <- sprintf("%.2f", .pn(SK_B) / .pn(COST))
.mw <- if (!is.null(.sc)) .sc$BCR[grepl("minimum wage", .sc$Scenario)][1] else "1.68"
BE_PP <- { .be <- .rdc("projections/bcr_breakeven.csv"); if (is.null(.be)) "4.1" else .be$`Break-even NEET reduction (pp)`[1] }
.pt <- .rdc("models/pass_through.csv")
PASS_PCT <- if (!is.null(.pt)) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*as.numeric(.pt$value)) else "45%"
NEET_RED <- if (!is.null(.pt)) sprintf("%.1f", 11.4*as.numeric(.pt$value)) else "5.1"
.mcs <- .rdc("projections/bcr_montecarlo.csv")
.mcw <- function(r) { if (is.null(.mcs)) return("most"); sprintf("about %d in 10", round(10*as.numeric(.mcs$`Probability BCR > 1`[r]))) }
.mcv <- function(r, col, pct = FALSE) { if (is.null(.mcs)) return("n/a"); x <- as.numeric(.mcs[[col]][r]); if (pct) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100*x) else sprintf("%.2f", x) }
.pa <- .rdc("models/followup3_A_programme_districts.csv")
PROG_DID <- if (!is.null(.pa)) .pa$`Difference in change (pp)`[.pa$Outcome == "NEET"] else "n/a"
PROG_P <- if (!is.null(.pa)) .pa$p[.pa$Outcome == "NEET"] else "n/a"
PROG_CI <- if (!is.null(.pa) && "95% CI" %in% names(.pa)) .pa$`95% CI`[.pa$Outcome == "NEET"] else "n/a"
BCR_TM <- if (!is.null(.sc)) .sc$BCR[grepl("Targeted at Madura", .sc$Scenario)][1] else NA
BCR_TP <- if (!is.null(.sc)) .sc$BCR[grepl("PKH households", .sc$Scenario)][1] else NA
.st <- .rdc("projections/bcr_steps.csv")
ONE_IN <- if (!is.null(.st)) .st$Value[grepl("^Girls exposed per girl", .st$Step)][1] else "14"
ENR_G <- if (!is.null(.en)) sprintf("%.0f%%", as.numeric(.en$rate[.en$unit == "East Java" & .en$sex == "Girls" & .en$year == "2025"])) else "71%"
.tg <- .rdc("models/targeting_scenarios.csv")
.tgv <- function(g) if (is.null(.tg)) "n/a" else sprintf("%.0f%%", as.numeric(.tg$`Out of school, girls 16-18 (%)`[.tg$Group == g]))
OOS_EJ <- .tgv("East Java"); OOS_M <- .tgv("Madura"); OOS_P <- .tgv("Poorest households (PKH)")
TAB <- file.path("..", "output", "tables", "t8_target_funnel.csv")
```

## Contents

::: {.toc-grid}
**1 · The problem**: who is left out, where, and at what cost

**2 · Theory of change**: what the programme does and why it should work

**3 · Projected returns (ex-ante)**: key assumptions and results

**4 · Key messages**

**Appendix**: regression results, methods and data
:::


::: {.notes}
The deck moves from the problem, to how the proposed programme is expected to work, to what it could return, and ends with key messages and policy recommendations. Technical detail is in the appendix.
:::

# 1 · The problem {.section-divider background-color="#00377C"}

## Girls have the same school attendance rate as boys, but their NEET rate is close to double {.smaller}

```{r f1a, results='asis'}
FIG("f1a_outcomes_by_sex_en.png", "70%")
```

[Data source: SUSENAS Maret 2025, East Java]{.datasrc}


::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Notes:** NEET: not in employment, education or training. Girls 15–24: 51% in school (boys 50%), 23% NEET (boys 13%), 25% employed (boys 37%). The gap opens at the transition out of school. SUSENAS Maret 2025, survey-weighted, 95% CIs.
:::


::: {.notes}
Girls aged 15 to 24 in East Java attend school at the same rate as boys. The difference appears after school: close to one in four girls is NEET, meaning not in employment, education or training, against about one in eight boys. This is why the programme focuses on the move from school into work or further study.
:::

## East Java's NEET gender gap is wider than the national average {.smaller}

```{r f19, results='asis'}
FIG("f19_national_benchmark_en.png", "76%")
```

[Data source: SUSENAS Maret 2025, all provinces]{.datasrc}


::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Notes:** Girls-minus-boys NEET gap: 10.3 points in East Java against 7.9 points nationally. Same survey, same definition, all provinces.
:::


::: {.notes}
The same comparison for every province shows that the gap between girls and boys is wider in East Java than in Indonesia as a whole. This is not only a national pattern.
:::

## The gap costs an estimated USD `r LOSS_BN` billion in forgone lifetime productivity {.smaller}

```{r f15, results='asis'}
FIG("f15_lifetime_loss_en.png", "80%")
```

[Data source: SUSENAS Maret 2025, East Java; earnings assumptions as in section 3]{.datasrc}


::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Interpretation:** About `r LOSS_GIRLS` girls are NEET in excess of the boys' rate. Each would be expected to earn about USD `r LOSS_PER` more over a working lifetime (present value) if she had the boys' NEET rate.
:::


::: {.notes}
This puts a value on the gap. About `r LOSS_GIRLS` more girls are NEET than would be at the boys' rate. Each would earn about USD `r LOSS_PER` over her working life, in today's money, if she were working. Together that is about USD `r LOSS_BN` billion. It shows what is at stake, not what the programme would recover.
:::

## Madura has higher NEET for girls and boys, with a similar gender gap {.smaller}

```{r f20, results='asis'}
FIG("f20_madura_en.png", "82%")
```

[Data source: SUSENAS Maret 2025, East Java]{.datasrc}


::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Interpretation:** Girls' NEET is 34% in Madura (Bangkalan, Sampang, Pamekasan, Sumenep) against 22% in the rest of East Java; boys' NEET is 23% against 12%. The gender gap is similar (11 vs 10 points), and fewer girls are in school (45% vs 52%). Madura is a priority area for a pilot.
:::


::: {.notes}
Madura stands out: NEET rates are higher for both girls and boys, and fewer girls are in school. The gap between girls and boys is similar to the rest of the province, so Madura needs both general and girl-focused support. This makes it a natural first area for a pilot.
:::

## Child marriage and outcomes: rest of East Java {.smaller}

```{r f24b, results='asis'}
FIG("f24_marriage_rest_en.png", "76%")
```

[Data source: SUSENAS Maret 2025, East Java]{.datasrc}


::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Notes:** Girls 15–24 outside Madura, by whether they married before 18, survey-weighted (95% CIs). Regression tests by region are in the appendix. Early pregnancy before 18 overlaps almost entirely with child marriage in this data, so only child marriage is shown. Association, not causation.
:::


::: {.notes}
Outside Madura, girls who married before 18 are much more likely to be NEET and much less likely to be in school. This is an association: the survey cannot tell whether marriage leads girls to leave school or the other way round.
:::

## Child marriage and outcomes: Madura {.smaller}

```{r f24a, results='asis'}
FIG("f24_marriage_madura_en.png", "76%")
```

[Data source: SUSENAS Maret 2025, East Java]{.datasrc}


::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Notes:** Girls 15–24 in Bangkalan, Sampang, Pamekasan and Sumenep. Fewer girls, so wider intervals. Association, not causation.
:::


::: {.notes}
In Madura the same pattern appears for school attendance, but few girls in the sample married before 18, so the estimates are less precise.
:::

## Married girls who work do more unpaid family work and less wage employment {.smaller}

```{r f21, results='asis'}
FIG("f21_employment_type_en.png", "72%")
```

[Data source: SUSENAS Maret 2025 (type of work); IFLS5 2014/15 (earnings)]{.datasrc}


::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Interpretation:** Among employed girls married before 18, 35% are wage employees (others 75%) and 31% are unpaid family workers (others 12%); 22% work under 20 hours a week (others 12%). Based on 78 employed married girls, so indicative. SUSENAS has no earnings; the appendix shows earnings by type of work for young women from IFLS5.
:::


::: {.notes}
Girls married before 18 who work are more often in unpaid family work or small own businesses, and less often in wage jobs. Typical monthly earnings are about Rp1.1 million for employees, Rp0.5 million for own businesses and nothing for unpaid family work, so the type of work matters as much as whether girls work.
:::

## Girls' NEET in East Java and the rest of Indonesia, 2024 and 2025 {.smaller}

```{r f23, results='asis'}
FIG("f23_trend_ej_vs_national_en.png", "70%")
```

[Data source: SUSENAS Maret 2024 and 2025, all provinces]{.datasrc}


::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Interpretation:** Girls' NEET (15–24) `r .chg("East Java","NEET_change")` in East Java and `r .chg("Rest of Indonesia","NEET_change")` in the rest of Indonesia; child marriage `r .chg("East Java","married_change")` and `r .chg("Rest of Indonesia","married_change")`; tertiary enrolment at 18–20 `r .chg("East Java","tertiary_change")` and `r .chg("Rest of Indonesia","tertiary_change")`. Both years use the same definition (any work in the last week, or temporarily absent from a job; not attending school). Survey trends cannot separate a programme from wider changes; a comparison of programme and non-programme districts is pending.
:::


::: {.notes}
Girls' NEET fell between 2024 and 2025 in East Java and in the rest of Indonesia, using the same definition in both years. Because it fell nationally, the change cannot be attributed to a provincial programme.
:::

## Senior-secondary enrolment rose faster in East Java than in the rest of Indonesia {.smaller}

```{r f25, results='asis'}
FIG("f25_secondary_enrolment_trend_en.png", "70%")
```

[Data source: SUSENAS Maret 2024 and 2025, all provinces]{.datasrc}


::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Interpretation:** Share of 16–18 year olds enrolled in senior secondary rose `r sprintf("%.1f", .enc("East Java","Girls"))` points for girls in East Java against `r sprintf("%.1f", .enc("Rest of Indonesia","Girls"))` in the rest of Indonesia (boys: `r sprintf("%.1f", .enc("East Java","Boys"))` against `r sprintf("%.1f", .enc("Rest of Indonesia","Boys"))`). The faster rise applies to both sexes, so it points to something affecting East Java's schools generally rather than a girls-specific programme. The district comparison can test whether programme districts drove it.
:::




::: {.notes}
The share of 16 to 18 year olds in senior secondary rose faster in East Java than elsewhere, for girls and boys alike. That points to province-wide changes in schooling rather than a girls-specific effect.
:::

## What changed for girls between 2024 and 2025 {.smaller}


::: {.tight-table}
```{r decomposition}
dc <- .rdc("models/followup3_B_decomposition.csv")
if (!is.null(dc)) knitr::kable(dc, align = "lrrrr")
```
:::

[Data source: SUSENAS Maret 2024 and 2025, all provinces]{.datasrc}


::: {style="font-size:0.56em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Interpretation:** Girls 15–24, same definitions in both years. The fall came mainly from more girls working (+2.8 points), not more girls in school (+0.4). NEET rose slightly among 22–24 year olds with a tertiary certificate, so the national internship programme explains little of the change in East Java. The share of working girls in trade or transport rose 4.5 points, against no change elsewhere, consistent with growth in informal and platform-based work.
:::


::: {.notes}
This table tests the explanations raised by the team for the fall in NEET. The fall came mostly from more girls working, especially in trade and transport, rather than from more girls in school. NEET did not fall among young women with a university degree, so the national internship programme is unlikely to be the main driver in East Java.
:::

## Programme districts compared with the rest of East Java {.smaller}

```{r f29, results='asis'}
FIG("f29_programme_districts_en.png", "84%")
```

[Data source: SUSENAS Maret 2024 and 2025, East Java; programme districts from UNICEF Indonesia]{.datasrc}


::: {style="font-size:0.56em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Interpretation:** Twelve programme districts pooled, against the other 26. Every indicator improved more in programme districts, but none of the differences is statistically significant: for girls' NEET the difference is `r PROG_DID` points (95% confidence interval `r PROG_CI`, p = `r PROG_P`). Lines on the bars show 95% confidence intervals. Programme districts were selected rather than assigned at random, and if the programme started before March 2024 part of its effect is already in the baseline, so this is a descriptive comparison, not an impact estimate.
:::


::: {.notes}
This compares the districts where the programme works with the rest of East Java, before and after. Programme districts improved more than the rest on every indicator, which is encouraging, but the differences are small enough that they could be chance. Programme districts were also selected rather than chosen at random, and we only have two years of data, so this is not yet evidence of impact.
:::

## Completing senior secondary is associated with 20 points lower NEET for girls {.smaller}

```{r f22, results='asis'}
FIG("f22_completion_left_school_en.png", "74%")
```

[Data source: SUSENAS Maret 2025, East Java]{.datasrc}


::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Interpretation:** Among 18–20 year olds who have left school, girls who completed senior secondary have a NEET rate of 41%, against 62% for those who did not. Adjusted for age and area (girls 18–24), completion is associated with a 20-point lower NEET rate (p&lt;0.001). For boys there is no observed difference. Keeping girls in school to completion is the programme's main lever.
:::


::: {.notes}
Among young women who have left school, those who completed senior secondary are about 20 points less likely to be NEET. For young men there is no observed difference. This is why keeping girls in school to completion is the programme's main lever.
:::

# 2 · Theory of change {.section-divider background-color="#00377C"}

## Evidence from Indonesia {.smaller}


::: {.vmid-l}
::: {.tight-table}
| Programme | Design | Result | Relevance |
|---|---|---|---|
| **PKH** cash transfer (Priebe &amp; Sumarto, 2025) | Quasi-experimental | Child marriage −3.5pp among girls | A cash component reduces child marriage |
| **PIP** education assistance (Ulfa &amp; Rezki, 2024) | Matching and IV | School participation +11.4pp (pooled, not girls-specific) | Anchors the effect used in the ROI, with a transferability assumption |
| **PIP**, girls' senior secondary (Caniago et al., 2021) | Observational regression | Girls' senior-secondary enrolment +24.6pp (adjusted association) | Targets the stage where girls drop out |
| **Vocational vs general secondary schooling** (Pritadrajati, 2022) | Quasi-experimental | Female LFPR +3.4pp (significant at 10%); income +5.6% (not significant) | Used only as an uncertain scenario in the ROI |
:::

[Data source: published evaluations (see references)]{.datasrc}


::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Interpretation:** In SUSENAS 2025, girls in PKH households have lower child-marriage rates than other girls (3% vs 4–6%), even though PKH targets poorer households. Consistent with the PKH evidence, though not a causal estimate.
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
These are the Indonesian studies the projection relies on. PKH, the national cash transfer, reduced child marriage among girls. PIP, education assistance, raised school participation, and that effect is the starting point for the projected return.
:::

## Theory of change


::: {.vmid-l}
```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 13
flowchart LR

  A1["Cash+: link to PKH / PIP,<br/>mentoring and<br/>marriage-delay outreach"]:::a
  A2["Digital and 21st-century<br/>skills in Double Track"]:::a
  O1["Child marriage<br/>delayed"]:::o
  O2["Girls stay in school<br/>and complete<br/>senior secondary"]:::o
  O3["Skills for<br/>work"]:::o
  R["Transition to work<br/>or higher education:<br/>lower NEET"]:::r
  I["Higher lifetime<br/>earnings"]:::r
  T --> A1
  T --> A2
  A1 --> O1
  A1 --> O2
  A2 --> O3
  O1 --> O2
  O2 --> R
  O3 --> R
  R --> I
  classDef t fill:#f4f4f4,stroke:#999,color:#333
```

[Data source: published evaluations and this analysis]{.datasrc}


::: {style="font-size:0.55em; color:#5a6b73; line-height:1.4;"}
- Cash transfers reduce girls' child marriage (PKH, Indonesia).
- Education assistance raises school participation and girls' senior-secondary enrolment (PIP, Indonesia).
- Completing senior secondary is associated with 20 points lower NEET for girls (this analysis).
- Skills to earnings is the weakest link: the Indonesian estimate is not statistically significant.
- Mentoring and outreach: international evidence for girls only.
- Cash+ links girls to existing PKH and PIP; no new transfer.
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
The programme has two parts. Cash+ links girls to PKH and PIP and adds mentoring and outreach to delay marriage. The skills component adds digital and 21st-century skills within Double Track. Both aim to keep girls in school to completion and help them move into work or further study.
:::

# 3 · Projected returns (ex-ante) {.section-divider background-color="#00377C"}

## Key assumptions {.smaller}


::: {.vmid}
::: {.assump-table}
| Assumption | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Reduction in girls' NEET | `r NEET_RED` points | PIP school-participation effect (+11.4pp, Ulfa &amp; Rezki 2024) × `r PASS_PCT` of girls who leave school before completing senior secondary being NEET (SUSENAS 2025) |
| Extra schooling for a girl kept in school | 3 years | Senior-secondary cycle |
| Earnings gain per year of schooling | `r MINCER_C` | IFLS5 wage return for women, controlling for region, parents' education and selection into paid work |
| Female earnings | Rp20 million/year | Below East Java minimum wage 2025, reflecting informal work |
| Probability of earning (employment rate, women 25–54, East Java) | `r EMP_C` | SUSENAS Maret 2025 |
| Earnings growth / discount rate | 2% / 3% per year | Career growth; 3% real, with 2% and 5% in sensitivity |
| Skills earnings premium (scenario only, not in the central case) | 5.6% for 10 years | Point estimate for vocational vs general schooling (Pritadrajati 2022), not statistically significant |
| Programme cost | USD 200 per girl | USD 58 per year for 3 years, plus 15% overhead; Cash+ links to existing PKH/PIP |
:::

[Data source: modelled projection (ex-ante)]{.datasrc}

:::


::: {.notes}
From here on the numbers are projections, not measured results. They show what the programme would return if these assumptions hold. Each assumption has a source, and the following slides show how much the result changes when they do not hold.
:::

## Every USD 1 invested could return up to USD `r BCR_SK` in lifetime earnings {.smaller}


::: {.vmid-s}
::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="44%"}
```{r f26, results='asis'}
FIG("f26_roi_bars_en.png", "100%")
```

[Data source: modelled projection (ex-ante); inputs as in key assumptions]{.datasrc}

:::
::: {.column width="56%"}
::: {.kf-list style="font-size:.66em; line-height:1.35;"}
- **Both channels together: USD `r BCR_SK` per USD 1.** USD `r TOT_B` in lifetime earnings per girl against a cost of USD `r COST`.
- **Conservative view, staying in school only: USD `r BCR_C` per USD 1.** USD `r RET_B` per girl, based on Indonesian causal evidence (PIP). The programme breaks even if it reduces girls' NEET by `r BE_PP` points; the evidence suggests `r NEET_RED`. At the 2025 minimum wage this rises to USD `r .mw`.
- **Skills channel on its own: USD `r SK_ONLY` per USD 1.** USD `r SK_B` per girl if the 5.6% earnings premium for vocational schooling in Indonesia applies; that estimate is not statistically significant, so this is the less conservative part.
- **Not counted in either:** delayed marriage, health, children's outcomes and fiscal returns. These are benefit-cost ratios, not fiscal returns to government.
- **The USD `r COST` per girl** covers three years of digital content, teacher training, mentoring, shared connectivity and marriage-delay outreach, plus 15% overhead; PKH and PIP transfers are existing entitlements.
:::
:::
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
Counting only the benefit of keeping girls in school, each dollar returns about USD `r BCR_C`. If the skills component also raises earnings, the return could reach USD `r BCR_SK`, but that part of the evidence is uncertain. Both figures count earnings only, so they leave out benefits such as delayed marriage and better health.
:::

[Data source: modelled projection (ex-ante); inputs as in key assumptions]{.datasrc}

:::

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Notes:** The central case is the retention channel. The targeted rows assume the programme's effect on school participation grows with the share of girls out of school in the group. In Madura more girls are out of school (`r OOS_M`, against `r OOS_EJ` overall), so the same spending moves more of them. In PKH households fewer girls are out of school (`r OOS_P`), consistent with PKH's school-attendance condition, so a programme there adds less. The skills row adds the uncertain skills premium; the others show earnings at the 2025 minimum wage, and the cost of adding a Cash+ stipend for the poorest 40%. With other assumptions varied one at a time, the central return stays between USD `r RANGE_LO` and USD `r RANGE_HI` (appendix).
:::



::: {.notes}
The same calculation under different assumptions. The return is higher in Madura, where more girls leave school, because the same spending then changes the path of more girls. It is lower in PKH households, where girls are already more likely to stay in school. It is also higher with the skills effect or at the minimum wage, and lower if a new stipend is added to the cost.
:::

## How likely is the programme to pay for itself? {.smaller}


::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r f28, results='asis'}
FIG("f28_bcr_montecarlo_en.png", "100%")
```

[Data source: modelled projection (ex-ante); 5,000 simulations]{.datasrc}

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.kf-list style="font-size:.64em; line-height:1.35; margin-top:1em;"}
- **Counting only the benefit of staying in school**, the programme returns more than it costs in `r .mcw(1)` runs. A typical run returns USD `r .mcv(1, 'Median')` per dollar; most runs fall between USD `r .mcv(1, 'Lower (5th pct)')` and USD `r .mcv(1, 'Upper (95th pct)')`.
- **Adding the skills effect**, it returns more than it costs in `r .mcw(2)` runs. The typical return is higher (USD `r .mcv(2, 'Median')`), but the spread is much wider, because the evidence on the skills effect is weak; in some runs it is assumed to lower earnings, which is why the bottom of the range is below zero.
- The typical run (USD `r .mcv(1, 'Median')`) is below our central estimate (USD `r BCR_C`) because some inputs, such as the discount rate and the employment rate, have more room to turn out worse than better.
:::
:::
:::



::: {style="font-size:0.52em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Notes:** we re-ran the full cost-benefit calculation 5,000 times (a Monte Carlo simulation). In each run, every uncertain input took a different value within its plausible range: the programme's effect on school participation (from half to one and a half times the PIP estimate), the share of school leavers who become NEET, the return to schooling and the skills effect (each varying by its statistical margin of error), and earnings, employment, the discount rate and cost (within the ranges in the appendix). The chart shows how often each result came up.
:::

::: {.notes}
To test how much the result depends on our assumptions, we re-ran the calculation 5,000 times, each time with different but plausible values for every uncertain input. Counting only the benefit of staying in school, the programme returned more than it cost in about 8 of every 10 runs.
:::

# 4 · Key messages {.section-divider background-color="#00377C"}

## Key messages {.smaller .bigtitle}

::: {.vmid-l}
::: {.kf-list style="font-size:.92em;"}
**1.** Girls in East Java have the same school attendance rate as boys but are close to twice as likely to be NEET, a wider gap than nationally, costing about USD `r LOSS_BN` billion in forgone lifetime productivity.

**2.** Completing senior secondary is associated with 20 points lower NEET for girls; child marriage with leaving school and more unpaid family work. NEET is highest in Madura, for girls and boys.

**3.** Most girls already stay in school (`r ENR_G` of girls aged 16–18 are in senior secondary), so a USD `r COST`-per-girl programme reaching all girls changes the path of about 1 in `r ONE_IN` and returns USD `r BCR_C` per dollar. Targeting Madura, where far more girls are out of school, raises this to USD `r BCR_TM`. The next frontier is the transition into work: if skills training also raises earnings, the return could reach USD `r BCR_SK`, an effect still to be tested in a pilot.
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
Three messages. The gap is at the transition out of school, and it is costly. Completing senior secondary matters, but most girls already stay in school, so a programme reaching everyone changes the path of only a minority. That is why the return is higher when the programme targets places like Madura, where more girls leave school, and why the next step is the transition into work, where skills training could add most, an effect that a pilot should measure.
:::

## Policy recommendations {.smaller .bigtitle}

::: {.vmid}
::: {.kf-list style="font-size:.84em;"}
**1. Target the transition, not enrolment.** Girls attend school at the same rate as boys, and senior-secondary enrolment rose faster in East Java than elsewhere in 2024–2025, but tertiary enrolment rose more slowly. Set targets on completion and the first job or further study, and pilot the skills component with an evaluation so its effect on earnings can be measured.

**2. Start in Madura.** NEET is highest and attendance lowest there: `r OOS_M` of girls aged 16–18 are out of school, against `r OOS_EJ` across East Java. Targeting Madura raises the projected return from USD `r BCR_C` to USD `r BCR_TM` per dollar.

**3. Link girls to PKH and PIP rather than creating a new transfer.** Indonesian evidence shows PKH reduces girls' child marriage, and girls in PKH households are already less likely to be out of school (`r OOS_P`, against `r OOS_EJ` overall). Linkage uses existing systems.

**4. Fund pedagogy and mentoring, not devices.** Internet use is already near universal, and devices alone did not raise learning in Uruguay.

**5. Measure the programme's own effect.** Programme districts improved more than the rest between 2024 and 2025 on every indicator, but not by enough to rule out chance. Build in a proper comparison from the start, and track whether girls move into wage employment rather than unpaid family work.
:::
:::


::: {.notes}
Five recommendations that follow from the analysis, from where to target to how to measure the programme's own effect.
:::

## Returns to schooling: specification and results {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}
**Wage-based** (IFLS5 2014/15, adults 20–60, estimated separately for women and men, weighted):

$$\ln(w_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 S_i + \beta_2 \text{Exp}_i + \beta_3 \text{Exp}_i^2 + \beta_4 \text{Urban}_i + \gamma_p + \phi_f + \phi_m + \delta \lambda_i + \varepsilon_i$$

$w$: monthly wage; $S$: years of schooling; Exp: potential experience (age minus schooling minus 6); $\gamma_p$: province fixed effects; $\phi_f$, $\phi_m$: father's and mother's education (fixed effects); $\lambda$: selection term from a first-stage model of working, in which children under 5 in the household predict whether a woman works but not her wage (Heckman two-step).
:::

::: {.tight-table}
```{r mincer-controls}
mc <- tryCatch(readr::read_csv(file.path("..","output","models","mincer_ifls_controls.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE), error = function(e) NULL)
if (!is.null(mc)) knitr::kable(mc |> dplyr::mutate(`Return per year` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * `Return per year`),
                                                   SE = sprintf("%.1f", 100 * SE)) |>
                                 dplyr::select(Sex, Model, `Return per year`, SE, N), align = "llrrr")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.58em; color:#7a7a7a;"}
**Notes:** The ROI uses the women's estimate with all controls (model 4, `r MINCER_C`). The consumption-based return from SUSENAS 2024 (5.6% for women; household per-capita expenditure regressed on schooling, schooling², age, age² and urban) is the low case in the sensitivity analysis.
:::

## Data sources {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.95em"}
- **SUSENAS Maret 2025** (BPS): NEET, school attendance and completion, child marriage, early pregnancy, type of work and hours, PKH receipt and digital access, for East Java and all provinces. East Java: 98,738 individuals, 12,599 aged 15–24, of whom 6,060 girls.
- **SUSENAS Maret 2024** (BPS): the 2024 comparison, and per-capita expenditure for the consumption-based return to schooling.
- **IFLS5 2014/15**: wages for the wage-based return to schooling.
- **Sakernas** (BPS): female labour force participation in East Java.
- **UMP Jawa Timur 2025**: benchmark for female earnings.
- **Published evaluations** of PKH, PIP and vocational training: the programme effect used in the return on investment.

All SUSENAS estimates are survey-weighted, with PSU/strata-clustered standard errors.
:::

## Definitions {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.95em"}
- **NEET (15–24)**: not in employment, education or training, built as not attending school (`R611`; 2024: `R610`) and not working in the last week or temporarily absent from a job (`R703_A`; `R704`, 2024: `R705`).
- **Married before 18**: age at first marriage (`R409`) under 18.
- **Senior-secondary completion**: highest certificate (`R615`) at SMA/SMK/MA level or above.
- **Type of work**: status in main job (`R706`); hours (`R707`).
- **Madura**: Bangkalan, Sampang, Pamekasan, Sumenep.

Several variables were renumbered between the 2024 and 2025 questionnaires (school attendance R610 to R611, temporarily absent R705 to R704, certificate R614 to R615, employment status R707 to R706); the activity block (R703) is the same in both years and both years are coded identically. The operational NEET definition does not separately exclude participants in non-formal training, which SUSENAS does not record.
:::
